Light can manipulate magnetic order and its excitations on ultrafast timescales, including through resonantly driven phonons. In antiferromagnets, light can also create correlated magnon pairs, or bimagnons. Unlike single magnons, whose damping has been measured and modeled in detail, little is known about the lifetime, interactions and decay of such correlated pairs: prior two-magnon measurements show broad linewidths or coherences that dephase within 200 fs. Here we pump the phonon-assisted two-magnon absorption of NiO with mid-infrared pulses, far below its bandgap, and probe the resulting magnetic dynamics at finite momentum with time-resolved resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). Upon photoexcitation, the one-magnon linewidth and energy are essentially unchanged, indicating that the long-range magnetic order is preserved without the photocarrier-induced demagnetization characteristic of above-bandgap excitation. A pump-induced two-magnon signal appears on the energy-gain (anti-Stokes) side of the spectrum. Its spectral weight peaks 4 ps after the pump, well beyond our 0.5 ps time resolution, indicative of a delayed growth likely due to momentum redistribution of the light-induced magnon pairs across the Brillouin zone. This two-magnon signal decays with a time constant of $28\pm11$ ps, exceeding the previously reported two-magnon dephasing time by more than two orders of magnitude. These results establish long-lived light-driven bimagnon correlations beyond the one-magnon state, akin to the higher-order correlations measured in ultracold gases.

The optical excitation of circular phonons has opened up non-equilibrium phenomena with no equilibrium counterparts, ranging from the generation of synthetic magnetic fields to the control of topological order or the manipulation of ferroaxial states. In this area, significant controversy has arisen on whether sizeable "true" magnetizations accompany circular phonons. Several confounding factors cloud the interpretation of the experiments, which are based on probing polarization rotation in the driven material. These range from the interpretation of the Faraday effect in non-equilibrium conditions to spurious nonlinear optical contributions in pump probe experiments. Here we resolve these ambiguities by measuring both polarization rotation inside the driven material and the stray magnetic field generated outside it with a proximate Faraday detector. For a 5 MV/cm mid-infrared drive, we observe a colossal polarization rotation inside a driven SiC crystal, similar to what was reported in previous work. Depending on the assumptions made, this could correspond to magnetizations as high as $μ_0 M = 0.3 T$ or as low as 4 $μT$. However, when measuring the magnetic stray field outside the driven sample we unambiguously determine that the magnetization in SiC is negligibly small ($μ_0 M \lt 0.001 T$).

☆ Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
Lucy Liu, Leon M. Kamp, Katia Bertoldi, L. Mahadevan
Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

☆ Metric random tilings: exact entropy and the diffraction of counted disorder

Tiling mathematics has twice become the language of a state of matter: crystals, then quasicrystals, whose thermodynamics are described by the random tiling of fixed shapes. There the counted variable is the arrangement rather than the geometry, although the metric is what chemical design sets and diffraction measures. Here we introduce metric random tilings, periodic networks of locked topology whose edge lengths fluctuate under exact face closure, so that the geometry itself is countable. Purpose-built counting engines enumerate Kepler's eleven uniform networks and divide them into seven zero-entropy ones and four carriers with positive metric entropy, each certified by an explicit construction. On the honeycomb, the densest carrier, all edge-length value domains considered carry extensive entropy, with the arithmetic class reaching $s = 0.544\,k_B$ per tile (fit band 0.53--0.58), the other two $\approx 0.2$. In diffraction, translational increase of the value domain leaves the entropy exactly invariant while the coherent fraction of the Bragg intensity at fixed patch size varies from $9\times10^{-4}$ to 0.58, following the Debye--Waller law of the amplitude flow. Metric disorder thus enters the exact-counting paradigm, and is identifiable in real materials by Bragg spots wrapped in metric halos.

Knowledge of phase stability is the first requirement for materials design, and predicting the conditions under which new materials can be synthesized has become a key capability of self-driving laboratories (SDLs). For inorganic materials, notably alloys, these predictions come from thermodynamic databases built with the CALPHAD method. Building a database, however, requires expert judgment at many steps, and because these decisions are rarely recorded, others can use a database but cannot regenerate or update it. Machines can already collect the data, build a first model with machine-learned interatomic potentials and refine it against experiments. The assessment itself, the sequence of judgments that turns these parts into a reliable database, is still carried out by human experts. We argue that it can be automated reproducibly only if the expert knowledge behind an assessment is encoded in formal protocols, so that an assessment delivers a record of its construction and not only its parameters. We introduce ORCHID-SAGE, a standard that organizes this record into reproducible and automatable protocols. In this first attempt, applied to Cr-Ni, the database was regenerated from its record by a script on a second machine, by an AI agent working only through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and by a refit from public sources only, with the same predictions. Recorded in this way, a database need no longer be fixed at publication but can be updated by AI agents as SDLs and other sources provide new evidence, while the judgment remains with people and on the record.

We first grow GaAs nanowire stems, and then convert Ga catalyst droplets into In droplets in situ. Axial heteroepitaxial growth of InSb can be realized through the In droplets on top of GaAs stems. We further find that a low flux suppresses radial growth, enabling linear length tuning from 0.8 to 2.6 micrometer with growth time, while diameter stays nearly constant. These InSb nanowires have a pure zinc-blende structure free of twins, stacking faults. Transport measurement reveals an electron mobility near 19000 cm2 V-1s-1. Moreover, the observation of quasi-ballistic transport, quantum dots, and Kondo correlations demonstrates the coherent quantum transport capability of the MBE-grown InSb nanowires. Our work provides a substrate-independent, self-catalyzed route for the controllable synthesis of high-quality InSb nanowires, establishing a robust material platform for high-performance InSb-based electronic and quantum devices.

☆ Controlled Growth and Disorder Mitigation of GaAs1-xSbx/InAs Core-Shell Quantum Wires

Compared with the well-studied GaAs-InAs system, incorporating Sb substantially reduces the lattice mismatch between the core and shell. Accordingly, both the nanowire crystal quality and device performance improved significantly. Increasing x from 0.15 to 0.35, the density of crystalline defects, such as stacking faults in the InAs shell, decreases by half. Moreover, the field-effect mobility increases from 3850 cm2/Vs to 4800 cm2/Vs, consistent with the reduction of the lattice mismatch. The incorporation of Sb makes the nanowire easier to pinch off via the gate voltage, enhancing the electric field tunability over the nanowire. Magneto-conductance measurements reveal Aharonov-Bohm-like oscillations, suggesting a phase-coherent tubular InAs shell. Our results identify lattice mismatch as a critical disorder source in core-shell nanowires and provide a practical route toward low-disorder core-shell quantum devices.

☆ Humidity-modulated Ostwald Step Rule in $\rm FAPbI_3$ Martensitic Transitions
Ping Tuo, Ju Li
Experimental observations reveal a dual role of moisture in $\rm FAPbI_3$ phase transitions. During fabrication at high temperatures, humidity improves the quality of the perovskite ($α$ phase) films, whereas at low service temperatures, humidity accelerates degradation of the photoactive $α$ phase into the photo-inactive hexagonal $δ$ phase. Despite extensive experimental evidence, the microscopic mechanisms by which moisture modulates phase stability and transition pathways remain unknown. Here, using large-scale atomistic simulations powered by an ab initio machine-learned potential, we reproduce the experimentally observed increase in the $δ$-to-$α$ transition temperature under increased humidity. Our simulations reveal a layered metastable intermediate along the Burgers transition pathway that exhibits a strong affinity for water. The competing water uptake of this intermediate and the $δ$ phase governs the humidity dependence of transition kinetics. These findings elucidate the dual role of moisture in perovskite phase transitions and demonstrate how environmental species can stabilize metastable intermediates and reshape transition pathways, providing an environment-dependent perspective on Ostwald's step rule.

Photon-induced near-field electron microscopy at 1030 nm shows that an Au particle in contact with NbS3 produces a near field of higher intensity and larger extent than an isolated particle of similar size, and that the hot spot at a contact is excited only when the incident polarization is parallel to the particle-NbS3 axis. Finite-difference time-domain simulations reproduce these observations and quantify the dependence of the coupling on the particle-NbS3 gap, the NbS3 thickness, and the dimension ratio of the NbS3 structure. Size-specific Au nanoparticles on NbS3 nanowires enhance the Raman scattering of rhodamine 6G by a factor of 1.8-4.2 relative to Au nanoparticles alone, with a detection limit of 10^-7 M. These results extend plasmonic metal/vdW hybrids to 1D vdW crystals and establish a multimodal approach that correlates the atomic structure of a metal/vdW interface with its nanoscale plasmonic response.

William F. Kent, Roberto does Reis, Gajendra Shekhawat, Emma Alexander, Vinayak P. Dravid
Atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) maps chemical composition at nanoscale spatial resolution, but the time required to acquire individual spectra limits hyperspectral imaging. Here, we introduce a convolutional-attentive conditional neural process (CACNP), a neural process architecture for reconstructing AFM-IR hyperspectral cubes from sparsely sampled spectra and a small set of structure images, each acquired at a selected wavenumber. The model is trained entirely on synthetic cubes generated from experimental infrared spectra and predicts both spectral intensities and their associated uncertainty. Validation on experimental datasets of poly(methyl methacrylate) and polystyrene particles embedded in epoxy demonstrates accurate reconstruction using only 5% of the available spectra, with competitive performance when compared to other methods. Inference takes less than 0.1 s on 128 X 128 hyperspectral cubes, supporting rapid reconstruction updates, while predictive uncertainty provides a basis for adaptive sampling of localized chemical features. This approach advances autonomous, high-throughput AFM-IR workflows and offers an architecture for accelerating other hyperspectral imaging methods.

♻ ☆ A Reduced Order Model for First-Principles Atomistic Simulations
Siu Wun Cheung, Youngsoo Choi, Jonas Kaufman, Daniel Osei-Kuffuor, Jean-Luc Fattebert
To leverage the redundancy between the electronic structure computed for various model parameters such as varying atomic positions, we present a data-driven modeling framework for Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory that bypasses the explicit optimization of electronic wavefunctions. We sample \textit{a priori} representative atomic configurations and construct a low-dimensional basis that efficiently approximates the electronic structure subspace. Subsequently, we employ this reduced basis in an iterative solver for the electronic single particle density matrix, thereby enabling the efficient determination of ground state without iterative wavefunction optimization. We demonstrate the accuracy of our approach in a Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics of a water molecule, showing that the resulting simulations accurately reproduce key structural properties, such as bond lengths and bond angle, obtained from full first-principles molecular dynamics. This work highlights the potential of data-driven approaches to develop low-dimensional electronic structure representations for first-principles simulations.
♻ ☆ How Does Incubation Affect Laser Material Processing?
Matthias Lenzner, Jörn Bonse
In the last decades, the subject of laser-induced damage (LID) moved from a topic of scientific interest toward laser material processing for technical applications. When using pulsed lasers, the cumulative effect known as incubation is one of the most fundamental features of the processing event. Incubation manifests by the fact that the critical fluence for LID (known as laser-induced damage threshold, LIDT) depends on the number of pulses N exciting one spot on the sample. In most cases, the threshold fluence decreases with N starting from the single-shot ablation threshold and remains constant for large N. No ablation or damage occurs for any N, if the fluence is kept below the multiple-pulse threshold. In contrast, examples where the LIDT increases with N have been reported. The latter effect is known as laser conditioning and is advantageously used when ramping up the power of high-power laser systems. Incubation has been described for many types of solids; the motivation for these comprehensive efforts is twofold. Firstly, one tries to prevent the damage of optical materials in the beam path of high-energy or high-peak-power lasers. Secondly, one deliberately uses this damage for the sculpting of components. In this chapter, we introduce the reader to the mechanisms of incubation. We are going to look at the parameters controlling LID and highlight the peculiarity of the parameter "number of pulses". We will give an overview of the experimental work done in a variety of materials. There are several physical and chemical mechanisms proposed that govern incubation, and there are several mathematical models to describe the behavior of threshold fluence and ablation rate in dependence on the number of pulses. In a few cases, the two classes of mechanisms are even related to each other. Eventually, we will show the implications that incubation has on real-world laser machining.

♻ ☆ Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms
Pawel Strak, Stanisław Krukowski
Ab initio extensive calculations were used to simulate the atomic stages of the vapor growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors (GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb) from their components. The structural and electronic properties of the stoichiometric polar surfaces of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors (GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb), i.e. metal- and nonmetal-terminated were determined. Adsorption of the components was simulated, shown to be atomic. At low coverages adatoms occupy H3 sites, considerably stabilizing the surfaces, at high coverage, the adatoms are located in the skewed on-top positions creating the first layer necessary for growth (with the exception of nitrogen admolecules). The second adlayer is adsorbed differently: on a Ga-terminated surface it does not create pyramid structures due to strong interaction within the first NM adlayer, thus preventing effective growth. On NM terminated Ga covered surface the second NM adlayer atoms create a stable pyramid structure which is an effective vehicle for surface diffusion. Growth of III-V semiconductors occurs via the attachment of the pyramids to steps by glue atoms, i.e. additionally attached NM adatoms. The NM glue atom connection process requires additional electrons, which leads to strong dependence of the process and the entire growth on the Fermi level at the NM terminated surface

♻ ☆ Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. II. Adsorption of nonmetal atoms (N, P, As, and Sb) on Ga-terminated surfaces
Pawel Strak, Stanisław Krukowski
Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the adsorption processes on Ga-terminated surfaces of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. The considered adsorbates are nonmetal species, i.e., nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony on wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e., GaN(0001) surfaces, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e., GaP(111), gallium arsenide, GaAs(111), and gallium antimonide, GaSb (111) surfaces. The cases investigated include single adsorbed nonmetal atoms and full coverage, i.e. theta=1 of these surfaces. The calculated results include the stable sites and the energies of the single adsorbed atoms: located at H3 sites at low coverage and in on-top positions at high coverage for GaP, GaAs and GaSb. At high nitrogen coverage, the N2 admolecules are formed, weakly attached to the surface. The calculated electronic properties of the single-adatom systems include the band diagrams of the slabs in real and momentum space, the energies of the quantum states. In addition, the overlaps of the quantum states of the nonmetal adatoms and the nearest topmost surface Ga atoms are given. The full coverage data include the atomic configurations and the bond energies of the adsorbed layers. The electronic properties include the above-mentioned data for single adatoms, together with additional properties related to interactions between adsorbed atoms. The evaporation stability analysis confirms that the adatoms stabilize the topmost Ga atoms against detachment because of the high energy barrier of DE > 3 eV which is further increased to DE > 4 eV by coverage located at H3 sites. Thus, growth simulations should employ unreconstructed Ga-terminated surfaces covered by nonmetal atoms located at on-top positions.

♻ ☆ Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VI. Surface diffusion on a nonmetal-terminated surface
Pawel Strak, Stanisław Krukowski
Ab initio calculations were used to simulate surface diffusion of adsorbates on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs (-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb (-1-1-1) surfaces. The mixed coverage consists of Ga adatoms in the first layer with a nonmetal atom attached above them forming a triangular-based pyramid. The pyramidal structures are stable during surface jumps involving rotations around one of the basal Ga adatoms. Thus, the diffusion proceeds via rotation (pivot) of the pair of the other basal Ga adatoms around an immobile Ga adatom moving them into new, originally empty sites. Using an energy-path determination procedure, the diffusion barriers were obtained as the difference between the initial site energy and the activated complex state energy. The detachment energy of the NM adatom was obtained assuming a final state in atomic and molecular form. The energy barrier for detachment to the atomic state is high for all atoms, on the order of 5 eV. For the molecular state these barriers are different: smaller for nitrogen, on the order of 1 eV, which is related to the high dissociation energy of the N2 molecule. For P and As the barrier is above 2 eV. For Sb it was not determined. Accordingly, the surface diffusion length is macroscopically large, indicating that all NM adatoms arrive at the steps.

♻ ☆ Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VII. Step kinetics
Pawel Strak, Stanisław Krukowski
Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the kinetics of attachment of new segments of the crystalline lattice (pyramids) at steps on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs(-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb(-1-1-1) surfaces. Diffusion species are gallium adatoms at high coverage or gallium adatoms connected with nonmetal atom creating stable pyramids. These pyramids arrive at the steps, and cannot be attached be directly because the Ga adatom at the pyramid base cannot be attached directly. Therefore they are incorporated into the step by additional nonmetal atoms glue atoms arriving from the vapor or detached from other segments of the surface terraces.

♻ ☆ FrOGS: Discrete Neural Sampler for Independent Alloy Configurations Across Chemical Conditions NeurIPS 2026
Kyucheol Min, Elyssa Hofgard, Tess Smidt
Predicting the thermodynamic properties of an alloy requires sampling its configurations across many chemical conditions and recovering free energies on a common absolute scale. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the standard tool, but it requires separate simulations at different conditions, and auxiliary free-energy methods such as thermodynamic integration are used to place results on a common absolute scale. Modern discrete neural samplers typically use reverse KL divergence as the objective and can be mode-seeking or biased. We present Free energy Offering Generative Sampler (FrOGS), a hybrid discrete neural sampler that couples an autoregressive model to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to be trained jointly under a single shared loss. FrOGS draws i.i.d. configurations, returns an unbiased estimate of the partition function, and gives consistent estimates of thermodynamic observables. We train a single model across a wide range of chemical conditions to produce estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale. FrOGS matches exact finite-size results on the 2D Ising model and reference phase diagrams for AgPd and CuAu, without mode collapse. We additionally compare to SEGAL, a published autoregressive baseline, and find that only FrOGS recovers the stability range of the CuAu$_3$ phase.

♻ ☆ Finite-temperature micromagnetic model bridging atomic- and macro-scale magnetism
R. Kiefe, J. S. Amaral
A multi-scale finite-temperature micromagnetic model is presented, based on the Landau-Lifshitz equation and the Bernoulli differential equation. This model accurately reproduces classic Maxwell magnetostatics of paramagnets for high temperatures and accurately reproduces standard micromagnetics described by the conventional Landau-Lifshitz model in ferromagnets. The Landau-Lifshitz-Bernoulli (LLBe) model can, by design, directly couple atomic-scale simulations with micromagnetics and output consistent predictions of bulk magnetic properties at finite temperatures, from below to above the material's Curie temperature. The LLBe model is validated against established solvers: MUMAX3 for zero-temperature micromagnetics, and FEMCE for high-temperature classic magnetostatics. We present an application of the LLBe model by simulating Heat-Assisted magnetic recording on a thin magnetic track with local heating, demonstrating the multi-scale finite-temperature capabilities of the LLBe.
♻ ☆ Field-free precessional magnetization dynamics in a multidomain magnet driven by light-induced strain
Héloïse Damas, Carl S. Davies, Tomasz Zalewski, Petr M. Vetoshko, Vladimir I. Belotelov, Andrzej Stupakiewicz, Andrei Kirilyuk
Ultrafast lattice excitation offers a route to controlling magnetization through magnetoelastic coupling, yet its ability to drive large-amplitude dynamics within pre-existing multidomain states remains less explored. Here, we show that a single 5-ps mid-infrared pulse induces a large-amplitude, reversible magnetic response in cobalt-doped yttrium iron garnet at zero applied magnetic field. Time-resolved magneto-optical microscopy reveals a transient reversal of the out-of-plane magnetic contrast within approximately 2 ns, followed by recovery of the initial state, while the labyrinthine domain morphology remains largely preserved. Concurrent polarization microscopy reveals a localized, long-lived strain-sensitive response and a propagating acoustic wave. The correlated structural and magnetic responses, together with micromagnetic simulations, support a mechanism in which transient strain modifies the magnetic anisotropy and drives precessional reorientation within existing domains. These findings establish single-pulse magnetoelastic excitation as a route to reversible, large-amplitude magnetization dynamics without substantial domain reorganization or an externally applied magnetic field.

♻ ☆ Electron--phonon matrix elements for hybrid functionals in the projector augmented-wave method: Eigenvalue projection, nondiagonal supercells, and Wannier interpolation
Qian Wang, Yu Xie, Yanming Ma
We present a finite-displacement approach to electron--phonon matrix elements that requires only eigenvalues and wave functions from the displaced calculations, for both norm-conserving pseudopotentials and the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method. Extending the eigenvalue-projectability approach, previously formulated for norm-conserving pseudopotentials, we reconstruct the displaced Hamiltonian from the displaced eigenvalues and from overlaps evaluated in the PAW metric of each displaced structure. Analytic terms constructed from the PAW dataset then yield the all-electron matrix element, without derivatives of the local potential or of the PAW strengths. The approach therefore applies in principle to any electronic-structure method available in PAW. To reduce the supercell cost, we combine it with nondiagonal supercells that sample the Brillouin zone equivalently to the primitive cell and recover the full matrix elements by crystal symmetry. Implemented in the ARES-EPC code, the method reproduces matrix elements from density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) and from VASP+phelel for seven materials with mean absolute errors below 0.5 meV. Nondiagonal supercells reproduce the diagonal-supercell results to the same accuracy and reduce the cost of the displaced calculations by up to a factor of 23. Through an interface to EPW, the norm-conserving matrix elements give an electron mobility of Si within 0.9% of that from DFPT. The HSE06 hybrid functional increases the mobility of Si by 13% relative to the PBE functional, because the lighter conduction band and the harder phonons outweigh the stronger coupling.

These results emphasise the relation between the two magneto-optical techniques, guiding the choice of probing wavelength for $\mathrm{Co_2Mn}$-based Heusler compounds, and provide a transferable approach for other magnetic materials.

♻ ☆ Curvature-Enhanced Polarization in Transition-Metal Dichalcogenide Janus Nanowrinkles

Strain-gradient engineering via out-of-plane wrinkling offers a powerful route to tune electronic and electromechanical properties in two-dimensional (2D) materials. Here, we systematically investigate the electronic and polarization response of wrinkled Janus MoSSe/MoSeS monolayers using density functional theory (DFT) calculations coupled with continuum elastica modeling. Exploring varying wrinkle sizes and compressive strain levels ($5\%$ -- $20\%$), we show that the global out-of-plane polarization follows a linear behavior when parameterized by the projected aspect ratio of the nanowrinkles. On this basis, we develop a physically grounded geometric model incorporating an effective 2D electromechanical coupling coefficient, which accurately predicts DFT polarizations without requiring higher-order nonlinear parameters. Atom- and orbital-resolved charge density analyses reveal the microscopic origin of this behavior: while the central Mo $4d$ projected weight remains approximately constant, local curvature drives continuous, chemically asymmetric charge transfer between the S $3p$ and Se $4p$ sublayer manifolds. Our findings establish clear geometric design rules for harnessing polarization in Janus monolayers for flexible nanoelectronics and optoelectronics.
♻ ☆ Intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in graphene stacks
Guillermo Parra-Martinez, Alejandro Jimeno-Pozo, Ady Stern, Jose Angel Silva-Guillén, Francisco Guinea
The effect of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in monolayer graphene has been thoroughly studied in the past. Its impact is commonly disregarded since the electronic structure of graphene is almost unaffected. Consequently, SOC has also been ignored in other graphitic systems. In this work, we calculate the intrinsic SOC in stacks of graphene layers from a model that includes all the valence orbitals of carbon as well as the intra-atomic SOC.The leading spin-orbit term in a graphene multilayer combines a Rashba-like spin-flip process with interlayer hopping. We find that this intrinsic term modifies the phase diagram and Fermi surfaces of finite rhombohedral stacks, and it leads to a distinct density-dependence of the magnetization in weak magnetic fields. This Letter shows that, unlike in the single-layer case, SOC has important consequences in multilayer graphitic systems and it should not be neglected when studying their physical properties.
♻ ☆ Thermo-elastic properties of hydrated epoxy-graphene nanocomposites from ensemble-based molecular dynamics simulations
Maxime Vassaux, Werner A. Müller, James L. Suter, Alexandros Anastasiou, Martin Simmons, David Tilbrook, Peter V. Coveney
Epoxy-based materials are inherently hygroscopic, absorbing moisture from the environment, which can significantly alter their short and long-term performance. The presence of graphene is often considered as a potential candidate to act as a microscopic barrier, mitigating the adverse effects of hydration on the matrix. This study investigates the impact of hydration on the glass transition and elastic mechanical properties of epoxy resins and their graphene nanocomposites, focusing on water content up to 5 %wt. Using large-ensemble molecular dynamics simulations, we analyze the temperature-driven glass transition and mechanical response of both neat epoxy and epoxy-graphene systems under varying hydration levels. Our results reveal a distinct threshold at 3 %wt water content: below this, hydration primarily reduces the glass transition temperature, while mechanical properties remain unaffected. Beyond 2 %wt, however, the mechanical properties deteriorate, highlighting a non-linear sensitivity to water uptake. Furthermore, we emphasize the critical role of ensemble size in ensuring the reliability of molecular dynamics predictions for such heterogeneous systems. Our simulations demonstrate that ensembles substantially larger than current state-of-the-art standards are necessary to achieve converged distributions of the predicted mechanical properties, particularly in highly heterogeneous hydrated epoxy-graphene nanocomposites. These findings provide novel insights into the hydration behavior of epoxy-based materials and underscore the limited potential of graphene to enhance their environmental resistance. This work also advances the understanding of structure-property relationships in polymer nanocomposites, offering guidance for the design of more robust materials in humid environments.
♻ ☆ Nodal magnon spin current at an antiferromagnet/altermagnet junction
Koki Mizuno
We investigate the thermally driven magnon spin current across a junction between a $d$-wave altermagnet (AM) and a ferromagnet (FM) or an antiferromagnet (AFM). The current consists of a component independent of the interface angle and an angularly dependent component with the $d$-wave form. For a sublattice-symmetric interface, the two junctions behave oppositely under reversal of the altermagnetic domain: in the FM/AM junction the angularly dependent component is odd and cancels on averaging over the domains, whereas in the AFM/AM junction the angularly independent component vanishes by symmetry and the angularly dependent component survives the domain average at a fixed Néel vector of the AFM. Both follow from a selective tunneling: a pair of spins bonded across the interface transmits magnons when the spins are parallel and not when antiparallel, which makes the AFM/AM junction a magnon valve: the configuration in which the bonded spins are antiparallel blocks the current up to the sublattice admixture of the magnons. We reveal the uniqueness of the altermagnet by comparing with the anisotropic antiferromagnet. The anisotropic tunneling is detectable as the sign reversal of the current between the interfaces normal to $[310]$ and $[130]$, and the valve reads the Néel vector of the altermagnet relative to that of the antiferromagnet through the magnitude of the current at a fixed interface.
♻ ☆ Hidden Quantum-Geometric Connection between Injection and Shift Currents
Mohammad Yahyavi, Tay-Rong Chang, Md Shafayat Hossain, Arun Bansil, Naoto Nagaosa, Guoqing Chang
Injection current (IC) and shift current (SC) are generally regarded as distinct nonlinear optical responses with different microscopic origins. Here, within the clean limit, based on an independent-particle interband description, we uncover a general hidden connection between the IC and SC responses. The generalized-derivative sum rule is used to show that the SC response separates into an injection-determined contribution associated with velocity asymmetry and a genuine shift-current (GSC) contribution associated with real-space wave-packet displacement. In systems with approximately linear electronic dispersion near the Fermi level, the corresponding tensor combinations of SC and IC can become effectively equivalent at low photon energies, governed by the same interband quantum-geometric dipole. Crystal symmetry can also eliminate the injection-determined contribution, enabling direct access to the GSC component. Extending our approach to second-harmonic generation reveals analogous response relations, suggesting a route toward a broader network of quantitative connections among the various nonlinear optical responses.
♻ ☆ Odd-Parity Altermagnetism Originating from Orbital Order

We propose a general symmetry-based strategy for realizing odd-parity altermagnetism by stacking two noncentrosymmetric monolayers in an interlayer antiferromagnetic configuration. In this setting, odd-parity spin splitting originates from nonrelativistic complex orbital order rather than spin-orbit coupling. By exploiting lattice symmetries, our framework enables the realization of both $p$- and $f$-wave altermagnets with nontrivial topological properties. Depending on the symmetry principles governing the bilayer stacking, the resulting altermagnet can host either quantum spin Hall or Chern insulator phases. Our work expands the landscape of altermagnetic phases and opens new avenues for discovering fascinating physical phenomena.

♻ ☆ Magnetic Quadrupole Lens and Current-Induced Quadrupolar Dynamics of Antiskyrmion

We demonstrate that antiskyrmions can serve as magnetic quadrupole lenses that focus or defocus electric currents traversing them. We showcase the antiskyrmion core as a focal point where electron beams converge for specific injection directions, leading to anisotropic and nonuniform current distributions. Thus the current-induced antiskyrmion dynamics is profoundly modified by the magnetic quadrupole lensing via the spin-transfer torque. By incorporating quantum transport and micromagnetic simulations iteratively, we self-consistently capture the coupled dynamics of conduction electrons and antiskyrmions. Our results unveil a quadrupolar antiskyrmion Hall effect that is highly anisotropic with respect to the current direction and can be effectively tuned by the spin-orbit coupling. In particular, the current focusing (defocusing) dramatically enhances (suppresses) the antiskyrmion speed while simultaneously reducing its Hall angle, thereby overcoming a key challenge for antiskyrmion racetrack memories. Our work establishes the intrinsic current lensing as a powerful mechanism for manipulating topological magnetic textures and opens new avenues for antiskyrmion-based spintronics.

However, realizing such control at room temperature (RT) in topological ferromagnets with high magnetic anisotropy (Ku) remains challenging. In square ice, domain-wall boundaries freeze the corners behind an arctic curve; strings of reversed arrows, unable to pass each other, give it Tracy-Widom fluctuations. In 3D, they pass around one another. Monte Carlo simulations calibrated on exact 2D results show that boundaries still sculpt an arctic surface in cubic ice, enclosing, by a lower bound, 3% of the box at the largest size. If local equilibrium holds up to it, it lies where the local field reaches the bulk Kasteleyn threshold. Its fluctuations are not Tracy-Widom along lines, and much closer than in 2D to independent strings.

♻ ☆ Influence of pairing and correlations on transport properties in three-terminal superconducting nanostructure
G. Górski, V. Pokorný, T. Domański
We study the local and nonlocal charge transport properties of three-terminal nanostructure, consisting of the correlated quantum dot embedded between two metallic electrodes and superconductor. Using the linear response theory, we analyze interplay of the induced on-dot pairing with the correlation effects, inspecting their influence on the conductance and thermopower. Our calculations predict negative values of the nonlocal conductance and reversal of the Seebeck coefficient when the quantum dot ground state is represented by the BCS-type singlet configuration. These phenomena are realized when the subgap charge transport is predominantly contributed by the crossed Andreev scattering. In contrast, on the doublet side, we obtain signatures for the Kondo effect manifested by the low-temperature enhancement of the charge conductance and clearly evident in the thermopower. Such temperature-dependent local and nonlocal transport properties can unambiguously identify the specific configuration of the correlated quantum dot and reveal the rich physics emerging in the doublet-to-singlet crossover region.

♻ ☆ Lyapunov-controlled thermalization: an exact real-time example
Jonas Loy, Jan C. Louw
A verified Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (KMS) relation, after a drive has ceased, is not sufficient evidence to prove equilibrium. We demonstrate this in a large-$N$ large-$q$ Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) quench protocol. Although all post-quench fermion correlators are exactly thermal, a second quench back to the initial Hamiltonian reveals hidden memory of the initial state. It is encoded in correlators connecting to times before the first quench. This memory is an extensive nonequilibrium (NEQ) witness with its decay rate being the Lyapunov exponent $λ_L$. Thus $λ_L$ sets the rate at which the state becomes effectively indistinguishable from a Gibbs state. Despite being a unitary interacting many-body system, the complete NEQ real-time evolution is obtained exactly in the large-$N$, large-$q$ limit, making the setup ideal for analytically studying thermalization.

♻ ☆ Quasi-1D Planar Magnetic Topological Heterostructure
Z. Z. Alisultanov
We theoretically introduce a quasi one dimensional magnetic heterostructure of alternating 2D topological and normal insulator strips. Such a structure can be realized by special fabrication techniques or may emerge naturally in twisted bilayers of certain transition metal dichalcogenides. Its low-energy physics is governed by a hybrid Hamiltonian intertwining the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Shockley models, with spin-momentum locking and local Zeeman splitting. Symmetry analysis places it in class AIII, characterized by chiral symmetry and a $\mathbb{Z}$ topological invariant. Computing the winding number from the block-off-diagonal structure of the Hamiltonian reveals topological phases characterized by invariants $ν= 0$, $1$, and $2$. Furthermore, a single magnetic defect acts as a sensitive local probe, whose in-gap spectrum provides a spectroscopic fingerprint to distinguish global topological phases. We show that the frequency-dependent optical absorption induced by such a defect exhibits distinct features in the topological and trivial phases, offering an independent, experimentally accessible local indicator of the global topological order. Extending the platform to a multilayer geometry uncovers a nonsymmorphic projective symmetry that gives rise to Möbius band topology.

A. Ramesh Chandra, Aaghaz Mahajan, Ainesh Sanyal, Mianqi Wang, Shubhadeep Chakraborty, Sudip Chakraborty, Shailesh Chandrasekharan, Rama Govindarajan, Akshit Goyal, Jonathan J. Heckman, Yasir Iqbal, Divya Jaganathan, Saumav Kapoor, Andreas Karch, Pushkar Khandare, Sandeep Krishna, Anupam Kundu, Alok Laddha, Tongyan Lin, Swarnendu Maity, Nilmani Mathur, Shani Nadir Meynet, Alessandro Mininno, Abhijeet Mishra, Vidur Niranjan, Abhishodh Prakash, Pratik Rath, Durbar Roy, Debargha Sarkar, Srikanth Sastry, Gary Shiu, Aninda Sinha, Thomas Van Riet, Praneeth Netrapalli, Suvrat Raju
We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.

♻ ☆ Neural and Tensor-Network Representations of $\mathbb{Z}_N$ Cluster and Dipolar-cluster SPT States
Seungho Lee, Daesik Kim, Hyun-Yong Lee, Jung Hoon Han
The $\mathbb Z_N$ cluster state is a paradigmatic example of symmetry-protected topological (SPT) order with $\mathbb Z_N\times\mathbb Z_N$ symmetry. We express its wavefunction and those of dipolar cluster states as a projector-based realization of correlator product states, which we dub the $P$-representation. The local projector $P$, also known as the copy tensor, can have multiple legs connecting a site to neighboring sites depending on the model and its deformations. We construct explicit wavefunctions of cluster and dipolar cluster states under deformation using the $P$-representation. The transition to the neural quantum state representations of the same state occurs by splitting the interaction matrices between $\mathbb{Z}_N$ spins into a pair of weight matrices. We derive these weight matrices explicitly for the cluster and dipolar cluster states, thus generalizing previous works on $\mathbb{Z}_2$ cluster states. The projector scheme then leads to the tensor product state (TPS) representation of the cluster-state wavefunctions. We benchmark the resulting TPS construction against conventional MPS representation using density-matrix renormalization group simulations and argue that the TPS could offer efficient representations for some modulated and deformed SPT states.

♻ ☆ Dynamics of $\mathrm{CP}^{N-1}$ skyrmions
Seungho Lee, Hyojae Jeon, Jung Hoon Han
We derive several exact results for the dynamics of CP$^{N-1}$ skyrmions with arbitrary $N$. Fractonic continuity equation is shown to hold for arbitrary CP$^{N-1}$ fluid implying the conservation of the topological charge and the dipole moment. Inclusion of the Gilbert damping modifies the continuity equation, resulting in the violation of the dipole moment conservation but not of the topological charge. Thiele's equation for the CP$^{N-1}$ skyrmion follows from the modified continuity equation. The Girvin-MacDonald-Platzman (GMP) algebra in the long-wavelength limit is derived for arbitrary CP$^{N-1}$ fluid. In the case of CP$^2$ skyrmions, we construct a finite-size skyrmion with dominant ferromagnetic moments. We find that its magnetic dipole texture carries a nonzero CP$^1$ charge equal to half the CP$^2$ skyrmion charge and argue that the topological Hall effect of electrons should exist due to their coupling to the ferromagnetic part of the CP$^2$ texture.

Fei Wang, Qiaohui Zhou, Hong Tang, Fan Zhang, Yanxing Li, Steven A. Hindmarsh, Chengkun Xing, Keyuan Bai, Sidra Younus, Ana M. Sanchez, Haidong Zhou, Chih-Kang Shih, Adrienn Ruzsinszky, Xin Lu, Jiang Wei
Probing anisotropic electron-phonon interactions (EPIs) is fundamental to understanding low-dimensional quantum materials, yet isolating their intrinsic signatures remains a challenge due to the confounding influence of extrinsic effects. Here, we resolve this ambiguity in quasi-one-dimensional $Ta_2$$Ni_3$$Te_5$ through a combination of angle-resolved polarized Raman spectroscopy and density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Anomalous four-lobe angular dependences were observed in Ag phonon modes, which deviate from the real-valued Raman tensor prediction. By employing a full quantum treatment incorporating detailed interaction mechanisms, we capture the qualitative characteristics and mode-to-mode diversity of the anomalous angular responses observed experimentally. The DFPT calculations further reveal mode-specific and momentum-resolved EPIs, providing microscopic support for anisotropic EPIs as the mechanism of anomalous Raman responses.

☆ Probing gluon saturation with forward heavy-flavor correlations in proton-nucleus collisions
Farid Salazar, Björn Schenke, Wenbin Zhao
We investigate heavy-flavor azimuthal correlations as probes of gluon saturation in high-energy $p$+$p$ and $p$+Pb collisions within the Color Glass Condensate effective theory. Heavy flavor has several advantages: heavy-quark production is especially sensitive to the small-$x$ gluon distribution of the target, while the quark mass suppresses collinear radiation. Further, the heavy meson carries a large fraction of the momentum of its parent quark, so that the meson pair follows the partonic kinematics more closely than for light hadrons. We present the first calculation of heavy-meson pair correlations over the full azimuthal range that combines small-$x$ evolution from an initial condition constrained by HERA data with Sudakov resummation near the back-to-back limit. It provides a good description of the $D$-$\bar D$ and $b$-hadron pair correlations measured by LHCb. In contrast to the light-flavor case, we predict, in addition to a suppression of the away-side yield in $p$+Pb relative to $p$+$p$ collisions by about $15\%$, a broadening of the peak by approximately $10\%$ to $25\%$ for Gaussian fits near $ΔΦ=π$, which makes heavy-flavor correlations a promising observable in the search for gluon saturation.

☆ Strangeness in the Chiral Mean Field model phase diagram
Mateus Reinke Pelicer, Nikolas Cruz-Camacho, Rajesh Kumar, Veronica Dexheimer, Jaquelyn Noronha-Hostler
We explore the phase diagram of the Chiral Mean Field model in the space of temperature and baryon, charge, and strangeness chemical potentials, focusing on the role of the strangeness direction. At low density, a negative $μ_S$ leads to finite strangeness in the nuclear liquid--gas transition and rotates the order parameter away from the purely baryonic direction. The critical mode remains baryon dominated over the $μ_S$ range considered, while the critical locus develops a strong parametrization dependence once multistrange baryons appear. At higher density, a separate first-order transition toward strangeness-rich hadronic matter appears only for one of the two parametrizations considered, emphasizing its interaction dependence. The high density transition reorganizes octet-dominated matter into decuplet-dominated matter: $Δ$ baryons provide most of the baryon-density discontinuity, while $Ξ^*(1530)$ baryons provide the largest contribution to the strangeness-density discontinuity. Its order parameter is dominated by the strangeness density, and its normalized direction in the $BQS$ space changes little with temperature even as the discontinuity vanishes at the critical point. The critical baryon chemical potential changes by almost $1$~GeV over $μ_S\in [-300, 300]$~MeV. We characterize both transitions using the fixed-temperature $BQS$ susceptibility matrix, the density discontinuity between the coexisting phases, and a generalized Clausius--Clapeyron relation. This work also accompanies the release of \cmfpp{} \texttt{v2.0.0} as part of the MUSES framework. The extension of the initial release includes, among other features, finite-temperature thermodynamics, new interactions and parametrizations, and susceptibility calculations based on a Jacobian method.

☆ Scalar and pseudoscalar glueballonia: do they bind?
Narmin Nasibova, Francesco Giacosa
We investigate the existence of molecular two-glueball bound states, so-called glueballonia, in pure Yang-Mills (YM) theory. We mainly concentrate on the scalar and pseudoscalar channels, thus studying scalar-scalar and scalar-pseudoscalar bound states, respectively. Near the onset of binding, when a bound state first appears just below threshold, a nonrelativistic framework is justified. We employ an attractive scalar-exchange Yukawa potential together with a smeared contact term contribution and determine the critical attraction required for binding. For two scalar glueballs, we use the scalar dilaton effective theory to determine the parameters of the non-relativistic potential: the Yukawa interaction is generated by t- and u-channels involving the exchange of one scalar glueball, while the repulsion emerges by the s-channel annihilation and contact interaction. Using lattice-YM input to fix the dilaton parameters, we find that the attraction is strong enough: the scalar glueballonium binds, and the result is quite robust with respect to parameter variations. In a minimal scalar-pseudoscalar extension, the Yukawa attraction is again given by the t-channel scalar glueball, while the crossed u-channel pseudoscalar exchange induces an attractive local contribution, making the pseudoscalar glueballonium also bind in pure gauge. Importantly, both the scalar and pseudoscalar glueballonia are stable in the YM vacuum. Next, we briefly comment on the pseudoscalar-pseudoscalar, scalar-tensor, and tensor-tensor channels: all these channels are attractive too and could form bound states, which, however, would be unstable in pure YM due to decay into two lighter glueballs. Finally, as a cross-check, our formalism confirms that Higgs-Higgs bound state does not form.

☆ Accelerating exact solutions of relativistic hydrodynamics and Levy-shaped freeze-out sources
Máté Csanád, Ágoston Benyó, Márton Nagy, Bence Szentkuti
Femtoscopic measurements in heavy-ion collisions indicate that the pion source is Lévy-stable rather than Gaussian, while the source radii still follow the hydrodynamic scaling $R^2\propto 1/m_T$. We call this coexistence the Lévy hydro puzzle. For a perfect fluid with $\varepsilon=κp$ and $p=nT$, flow and pressure form a closed system, and density and temperature can be ``dressed'' by an arbitrary comoving function, generalising a freedom known from Hubble-type solutions to arbitrary flows. We show that, at nonzero pair momentum, the source is bounded by the pressure on the freeze-out hypersurface, so its tail can never be heavier than the pressure tail. This yields a criterion for power-law source tails with two routes: either the outer flow is ultra-relativistic and the temperature grows at least linearly (Hubble-type solutions), or the flow is slow, the temperature uniform, and the proper acceleration falls off as $1/r$. We present a new family of relativistic, accelerating, self-similar potential flows ($λ$-PF) and a new dressing of Gubser's flow. The acceleration of $λ$-PF generates no power-law tail, but with a Hubble-type dressing its source tail is Lévy-stable in a range of parameters, generalising the Hubble-type Lévy source to accelerating cores. The isothermally dressed Gubser flow realises the $1/r$ route: its tail exponent lies outside the Lévy-stable range, but over the measured range it gives Lévy-like sources with $1/R^2$ linear in $m_T$. Thus Lévy-like sources and the hydrodynamic $m_T$ scaling are compatible in perfect-fluid hydrodynamics, but hydrodynamics does not create the power-law tail: it is either inherited from a power-law pressure, requiring a $1/r$ acceleration, or put in through the dressing. We outline extensions towards non-spherical geometries and elliptic flow.

Accounting for finite-size effects, we design driving protocols that exploit diverging susceptibilities to enhance signal-to-noise ratios in parameter estimation using experimentally relevant generators. We show that the excited-state criticality provides a metrological advantage through single-mode bosonic squeezing in regimes that circumvent the 'death of adiabaticity', limiting conventional critical quantum metrology with ground-state criticality.

☆ A Non-Relativistic Model of Heavy Quarkonium
Christian Farina
We develop a non-relativistic, spin-dependent, phenomenological model of heavy quarkonium. The model is based on a hydrogen-like Schrödinger equation derived from a spin-dependent Hamiltonian that includes a hyperfine spin--spin interaction term. The resulting system is solved using matrix mechanics by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian to obtain the energy spectrum. The energies are further optimized using variational methods. Spin--orbit corrections are included at first order in perturbation theory. The resulting spectrum shows good agreement with experimental data for conventional heavy quarkonium states. The framework combines matrix mechanics, variational methods, and perturbation theory, and is therefore suitable for students familiar with quantum mechanics.

We found the additional narrower constraints for the NS radius due mainly to the $t,\varphi$ correlations and surface contributions and NS surface deformation. The adiabaticity conditions for application of the linear perturbation theory is carried out for several neutron stars with a strong gravity and relatively large rotation periods.

The resulting posterior provides substantially improved constraints for different baryon--meson couplings and non-linear meson self-interactions, which are consistent with the current astrophysical observations of neutron star masses, radii and tidal deformability parameters.

Together, these measures link nuclear correlations to the selection of active modes and candidate excitation operators and to the design of quantum register layouts, offering guidance for the development of hybrid quantum-classical calculations of nuclei.

We present results on the Mellin moments of the unpolarized parton distribution function (PDF) of the pion and kaon up to the fourth order. We reconstruct the valence pion and kaon PDFs using the connected contributions to the three Mellin moments. We compare our results on the Mellin moments and the reconstructed PDFs with other lattice QCD and phenomenological determinations.
comment: Expanded version published in Phys. Rev. D 113, 11, 14524 (2026), 19 pages and 16 figures
♻ ☆ Cross-Environment Diagnostics for New Physics in Proton-Proton and Heavy-Ion Collisions
Yi Yang
Particle-physics searches and heavy-ion measurements probe many of the same final states, but their results are often interpreted separately. We propose testing new contributions hidden beneath established resonances by requiring a common candidate hypothesis across collision systems. Different nuclear responses change the relative populations of unresolved components and link proton-proton production and mass distributions to nuclear modification and azimuthal anisotropy. We derive these relations and, for component mass distributions of the same shape within each system, a relation between total nuclear modification and the calibrated shift in the mean invariant mass in which quarkonium yield suppression cancels. The candidate component's nuclear modification remains an input to this test. An example near the $Υ(1S)$ follows a component absorbed into proton-proton fits into nuclear observables; for the specified responses, its fraction rises from five percent in proton-proton collisions to thirteen percent in nucleus--nucleus collisions. These results provide conditional consistency tests linking particle and nuclear measurements. Their use requires constrained candidate responses and controlled quarkonium and detector uncertainties; the statistical gain from adding nuclear data must be evaluated with the actual event samples.
comment: Major revision. The manuscript has been reframed as a model-independent heavy-ion diagnostic for new particles hidden beneath known quarkonium resonances. No claim of evidence for a new state is made. Added a reorganized template-level framework, heavy-ion bias scaling, a Upsilon(1S) stress-test example, sensitivity maps, limitations, updated references, and an AI-assistance declaration
♻ ☆ How acausal equations emerge from causal dynamics
Lorenzo Gavassino
We construct a causal and covariantly stable kinetic model whose spectrum at real wavenumbers $k$ reproduces any rest-frame stable dissipative dispersion relation $ω(k)$ via suitable initialization of the microscopic degrees of freedom. Macroscopic observables can therefore obey arbitrary linear evolution equations (including forms that would be acausal if taken as fundamental), while the underlying dynamics remains causal, and all apparent propagation is encoded in the initial data. This provides an explicit counterexample to the idea that microscopic causality alone constrains the analytic form of dispersion relations at real $k$. In particular, bounds on transport coefficients based solely on the analytic structure of $ω(k)$, such as the hydrohedron bounds, require additional assumptions about the region in the complex $k$-plane where $ω(k)$ corresponds to physical modes.
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, published in PLB (see https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370269326009822?via%3Dihub)
♻ ☆ Retarded Correlators of Charge Transport in a Magnetic Field
Xuan Zhao, Qiuze Sun, Yi Wang, Jin Hu
We study charge transport in a magnetized relativistic plasma using kinetic theory within the relaxation-time approximation. By exactly solving the linearized Boltzmann equation in a uniform magnetic field, we obtain an analytic solution for the distribution function in terms of Bessel functions. Using this solution, we compute the full set of retarded current-current correlators and verify the Ward identities. In the hydrodynamic limit, we extract the charge diffusion modes, demonstrating that the transverse diffusion coefficient is strongly suppressed by the magnetic field, scaling as $1/B_0^2$ in the strong-field regime, while the longitudinal diffusion remains unaffected. Furthermore, we analyze the non-hydrodynamic branch cuts in the complex frequency plane, determining their kinematic thresholds and identifying the underlying wave-particle interactions as longitudinal Landau damping and transverse cyclotron damping.
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures; version published in JHEP; comments welcome
♻ ☆ Levy-shaped femtoscopic sources from an exact solution of relativistic hydrodynamics
Bence Szentkuti, Mate Csanad
An important goal of high-energy physics is to better understand the spacetime structure of particle emitting sources created in heavy-ion collisions. For a fraction of a second, a special form of matter, the so-called quark-gluon plasma (QGP), is created, which can be examined with the toolkit of femtoscopy. With the measurement of correlation functions it was determined that Lévy distributions describe the shape of hadron (pion) emission sources at freeze-out the most accurately; however, based on hydrodynamics Gaussian distributions are typically expected. In this article we showcase an exact solution of the equations of relativistic hydrodynamics, which aims to resolve this puzzle by providing Lévy distributions directly from hydrodynamics. A detailed analysis reveals whether the predictions of this solution are in accordance with observations; in particular, the effective temperatures from angle-averaged transverse mass distributions and the femtoscopic radii from two-particle momentum correlation functions are analyzed.

♻ ☆ Quantum Simulation of QCD in Axial Gauge
Xiaojun Yao
We study quantum simulation of SU(3) non-Abelian gauge theory dynamically coupled with fundamental fermions in $3+1$ dimensions by employing the lattice Hamiltonian in axial gauge under fixed boundary conditions, which avoids Gauss's law constraints. The temporal component of the gauge field is analytically solved in terms of independent field degrees of freedom and a lattice regulated Green's function. The axial gauge condition is trivially maintained in time evolution, even under Trotterization. The gauge field degrees of freedom are expressed in the local field basis and can be efficiently transformed into the canonical conjugate momentum basis by local quantum Fourier transforms. We prove the number of qubits needed for describing all states up to an energy $E$ with an accuracy $ε$ on a lattice of volume $V$ at bare coupling $g$ is bounded as $16n_A V + 12n_f V$, where $n_A \approx \log_2 (\frac{64 E' V^{4/3}}{π^2ε} + \frac{32\sqrt{2}g n_f E'^{1/2} V^{7/6}}{\sqrt{3}π^3ε^{1/2}} ) $ is the number of qubits needed for each independent gauge field per site with a shifted energy $E'$, and $n_f$ denotes the number of fermion flavors. We then analyze a quantum algorithm for time evolution that is based on Trotterization, quantum Fourier transform, and Jordan-Wigner transformation, for which quantum circuits can be explicitly constructed under arbitrary gauge field truncation and digitization. We find the numbers of CNOT and single-qubit rotation gates scale as $O(n_A^4 V^{4/3}) + O(V^{5/3})$ and $O(n_A^4 V^{4/3})$, respectively, per Trotter step for fixed $n_f\leq 6$. Together with the bounded Trotterization error, we conclude that quantum resources needed for simulating real-time dynamics of lattice QCD scale polynomially with volume, energy, time, accuracy, and bare Hamiltonian parameters.

♻ ☆ On the Nucleon Effective Mass in Neutron Stars Cooling
Yuuki Sugiyama, Akira Dohi
The cooling of neutrons stars, which are composed of ultra-high-density nuclear matter, strongly depends on the equation of state because the dominant cooling sources are neutrinos produced in their interiors. Here, we investigate the cooling properties of neutron stars, focusing on effective nucleon masses, whose impacts have been recently examined in supernova explosion and proto-neutron star cooling. The uncertainties of effective masses originate from the difference in the attractive interaction of scalar meson and the definition of the Dirac and Landau masses. At first, we employ so-called Walecka models that allow these two masses to be introduced within a unified framework and evaluate the resulting cooling curves. Based on the Walecka model, we compute the emissivity of the neutrons and the direct Urca process and their cooling curves. We demonstrate that the Dirac and Landau masses affect cooling of massive neutron stars, although most previous cooling simulations do not distinguish them. We also perform cooling simulations with two realistic equation of states based on relativistic mean-field (RMF) theory, whose differences arise from properties of only effective masses among characteristic parameters. These results are broadly consistent with those obtained from the Walecka models, indicating that the treatment of effective nucleon masses may be an important source of uncertainty in neutron-star cooling.

♻ ☆ Space-time Areas and Hadronization Studies
S. Abachi, C. Buchanan
Space-time area laws play a fundamental role in modeling strongly interacting phenomena, such as in relativistic string models, QCD on the lattice, and in hadronization modeling. For the latter, an exact expression for relevant space-time areas related to the final state hadronic events for hadrons of any mass is calculated. Usage of this expression in the UCLA hadronization model helps validate its space-time area law (STAL) principle and unifies the treatment of heavy and light hadrons via a single fragmentation function.

☆ Exclusive cross section measurements of $^{12}$C(n,p$_\text{n}$) and $^{12}$C(n,d$_\text{n}$) reactions
A. Wantz, A. N. Kuchera, W. F. Rogers, T. Baumann, C. Boothby, M. Devlin, N. Frank, P. Gueye, K. J. Kelly, S. A. Kuvin, A. LaRochelle, T. Redpath, T. Tran Nguyen, J. R. Winkelbauer
A single-crystal chemical vapor deposited (sCVD) diamond detector was used at LANSCE to measure neutron-induced reactions on carbon. Neutrons with a broad energy spectrum were produced via spallation. Relative cross sections are reported from above threshold up to 26 MeV incident neutron energy for $^{12}$C(n,p$_2$)$^{12}$B, up to 23 MeV for $^{12}$C(n,p$_{3+4}$)$^{12}$B, and up to 35 MeV for $^{12}$C(n,d$_1$)$^{11}$B and $^{12}$C(n,d$_2$)$^{11}$B, all of which represent the highest-energy measurements for these reactions to date, and the first measurement for (n,d$_2$). Cross sections for $^{12}$C(n,p)$^{12}$B$_\text{total}$ and $^{12}$C(n,d)$^{11}$B$_\text{total}$ are also reported from sums of the partial cross sections. These measurements are compared with recent data from EXFOR as well as TALYS calculations. These data are useful for future nuclear data evaluations and can be used as cross section inputs for data-based simulation packages.
☆ Probing gluon saturation with forward heavy-flavor correlations in proton-nucleus collisions
Farid Salazar, Björn Schenke, Wenbin Zhao
We investigate heavy-flavor azimuthal correlations as probes of gluon saturation in high-energy $p$+$p$ and $p$+Pb collisions within the Color Glass Condensate effective theory. Heavy flavor has several advantages: heavy-quark production is especially sensitive to the small-$x$ gluon distribution of the target, while the quark mass suppresses collinear radiation. Further, the heavy meson carries a large fraction of the momentum of its parent quark, so that the meson pair follows the partonic kinematics more closely than for light hadrons. We present the first calculation of heavy-meson pair correlations over the full azimuthal range that combines small-$x$ evolution from an initial condition constrained by HERA data with Sudakov resummation near the back-to-back limit. It provides a good description of the $D$-$\bar D$ and $b$-hadron pair correlations measured by LHCb. In contrast to the light-flavor case, we predict, in addition to a suppression of the away-side yield in $p$+Pb relative to $p$+$p$ collisions by about $15\%$, a broadening of the peak by approximately $10\%$ to $25\%$ for Gaussian fits near $ΔΦ=π$, which makes heavy-flavor correlations a promising observable in the search for gluon saturation.

CUPID is a next-generation tonne-scale cryogenic experiment that will search for the neutrinoless double beta decay $(0νββ)$ of $^{100}$Mo. It will be located at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Italy) and will employ the cryogenic calorimetric technique to reconstruct the energy deposited in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ crystals, in which the isotope of interest is embedded. Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $μ$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

☆ Tau polarization, new physics and CP violation in $ν_τ$-nucleus hyperon production
E. Hernández, J. Nieves, J. E. Sobczyk
Charged-current interactions of the $τ$ neutrino are the least constrained sector of the Standard Model (SM) flavour structure, and the polarisation of the produced $τ$ lepton probes new-physics (NP) couplings, including CP-violating ones. Hyperon and charmed-baryon production gives access to the $u\to s$ and $d\to c$ transitions, but any measurement would be made on nuclei, which calls for a proper treatment of nuclear effects. We therefore study the sequential reactions $ν_τ\,{}^A Z\toτ^-(\toπ^-ν_τ)\,Λ_c^+ X$ and $\barν_τ\,{}^A Z\toτ^+ (\toπ^+\barν_τ)\,ΛX$ within the impulse approximation. The energy and angular distributions of the pion, which encode the $τ$ polarization, are derived for an arbitrary nuclear hole spectral function. As for free nucleons, an azimuthal pion asymmetry with respect to the plane spanned by the neutrino and the outgoing baryon is shown to remain. This is a CP-odd observable that vanishes in the SM, so that a nonzero value would signal CP violation irrespective of the hadronic form factors. Local Fermi gas results for ${}^{16}$O show that nuclear effects lower the reaction thresholds but leave the pion distributions, and hence the polarization information, close to their free-nucleon form. For representative NP scenarios the predicted asymmetries are at the percent level or below, with a magnitude that, in the $Λ$ channel, depends strongly on the transition form factors.

♻ ☆ Corrections to the Smoothness and On-Shell Approximations in Femtoscopy and Coalescence
Isaac G. Smith, Kfir Blum
Relativistic heavy-ion collisions produce femtometer-scale sources whose space-time structure can be constrained using two-particle femtoscopic correlations. Standard implementations rely on the smoothness and on-shell approximations, which effectively remove the relative momentum dependence of the particle emission function. We explore the validity of these approximations by deriving model-independent expansions that quantify the leading corrections for femtoscopy and coalescence with arbitrary sources and final-state interactions. The resulting first- and second-order correction terms can be evaluated with essentially the same numerical complexity as the usual Koonin-Pratt expressions; for angle-averaged correlations the first-order contributions vanish by symmetry. This version of our paper corrects a numerical error in a previous version. We find that the smoothness corrections are numerically larger than previously reported.

☆ KNO functions for dipole-dipole scattering from large Pomeron loops: log-normal tails and a test in exactly solvable models
Michael Roa
The sum of large Pomeron loops in QCD, based on the $t$-channel unitarity and on the solution of the Balitsky-Kovchegov (BK) equation in the saturation region, has been combined with the AGK (Abramovsky, Gribov and Kancheli) cutting rules to obtain multiplicity distributions with KNO (Koba, Nielsen and Olesen) scaling and an entropy equal to the logarithm of the gluon structure function. We reexamine these distributions for the BK amplitude and for dipole-dipole scattering. The KNO functions that follow from the Gaussian representation of the asymptotic series have log-normal and not Gaussian tails, $\lnΨ_{\rm BK}\simeq-\frac{1}{2}\ln^2ξ$ and $\lnΨ_{\rm dd}\simeq-\frac{1}{4}\ln^2ξ$, and we give them in closed form in terms of the Lambert function. They are log-normal mixtures of the distributions of one and two BFKL cascades, and the summation is not unique. The KNO scaling requires that power-like factors in the coefficients of the series be discarded, and the alternative contour representation leads to functions that change sign. We then test the approach in two exactly solvable models in zero transverse dimensions. In the unitary toy model we confirm that the resummed series reproduces the exact $S$-matrix to within 2.5-10%, while the $S$-matrix changes by many orders of magnitude. Nevertheless, the multiplicity distribution obtained from the same series with the AGK rules agrees with the exact one only as long as both cascades are dilute. At higher energies the exact mean grows as a power of rapidity, the KNO scaling is absent, and the entropy in the rest frame of the target grows as one half of the logarithm of the mean multiplicity. The amplitude is determined by rare configurations of the cascades and the multiplicity by the typical ones, so that the agreement of the amplitudes does not validate the multiplicity distributions.

☆ Anti-periodic Gravitino and Dirac Effective Operators
Karim Benakli
Introducing a preserved $U(1)_R$ symmetry forbids gravitini Majorana masses while allowing a Dirac mass. We investigate how a Dirac mass for gravitini can be described by an effective operator in $N=1$ superspace, in analogy with the well-known Dirac gaugino mass. We find that the corresponding spin-$3/2$ bilinear operator can be expressed in terms of gauge-invariant gravitino curvature superfields coupled through a nonlocal kernel involving an inverse d'Alembertian. We study this construction in minimal five-dimensional supergravity compactified on $S^1/\mathbb Z_2$. The gravitino satisfies anti-periodic boundary conditions induced by a Scherk-Schwarz twist. The physical Kaluza-Klein Dirac masses then appear as poles in the two-point functions of the curvature superfields associated with sources localized at the endpoints. Separation of physical and gauge modes relates these propagators to a quadratic fermionic kernel represented by a $16\times16$ matrix. Its elements match the fermionic components of two invariants written in $N=1$ superspace, including their spinor contractions and normalization. This matching is carried out on a fixed background with a nonzero radion auxiliary field.

☆ Silent Heavy Fields: An Exclusion Rule for the Cosmological Collider
Shuntaro Aoki, Zhehan Qin, Masahide Yamaguchi, Yuhang Zhu
The cosmological collider uses oscillatory signatures in primordial correlators to probe heavy fields during inflation. This probe has blind spots, as heavy fields can keep ticking in time while remaining silent in the correlators. In this letter, we derive an exclusion rule under which cosmological collider signals vanish. The rule covers two classes of diagrams where a de Sitter invariant heavy sector couples covariantly to a single external field at one vertex. We first prove it for exchanges mediated by the two-point function of the heavy sector to all loop orders, using a spectral decomposition followed by a field redefinition. The result then extends to one-loop polygons by matching their oscillatory contributions onto those of the first class. The approximate signals of previously studied processes that fall into these classes must therefore be revisited. As a nonvanishing example, we derive the leading signal of a triangle loop for the first time in a toy model motivated by chemical potentials.
